questions.question: Describe the compass-and-wire demonstration and explain what a solenoid is, including how its poles can be reversed.
questions.expected_answer: A plotting compass placed beside a straight wire swings to lie across the wire when current flows and returns to north when the current stops, showing that a current produces a magnetic field in circles round the wire, as Oersted found in 1820. Winding the wire into a coil adds the fields of all the turns inside it, so the coil, called a solenoid, behaves like a bar magnet with a north end and a south end; the compass points into one end and out of the other. Reversing the cell reverses the current and swaps the poles, which no permanent magnet can do. Without a core the solenoid is weak; an iron core makes it strong.

questions.question: Explain how to build the electromagnet, why the iron core makes it so much stronger, and the three ways its strength can be increased.
questions.expected_answer: Leave a free end of wire, wind about fifty tight neat turns round an iron nail all in one direction, leave another free end, scrape the insulation off the tips and connect through a push switch to a cell; pressing the switch makes clips jump to the nail and releasing drops them. The coil's field lines up the domains in the iron so the nail becomes a strong temporary magnet whose field adds to the coil's, multiplying it hundreds of times; soft iron is used so that it lets go when the current stops. Strength increases with more turns, with more current from an extra cell, which also heats the wire, and with an iron rather than air or copper core; turns wound in opposite directions cancel.

questions.question: Compare a permanent magnet with an electromagnet for the scrap-crane task and give examples of electromagnets in everyday devices.
questions.expected_answer: A permanent magnet is always on, so it lifts steel but never releases it, cannot be adjusted and grabs tools and loose steel nearby. An electromagnet works only while the switch is closed, so the operator can lift, swing and drop; its strength can be changed by changing the current and it can be reversed. Its disadvantage is that it needs electricity and fails if the supply fails, so real crane magnets have their own generator and loads are never swung over people. Electromagnets are found in electric bells, buzzing door locks, relays, loudspeakers, hospital scanners, maglev trains and electric motors, which are electromagnets switched in turn.
